title: India is the Place for Legal Outsourcing: Pangea3 MD
author: Samar Srivastava

dom.t: Legal outsourcing: Commercial growth need not advance workers

st.t: Legal outsourcing: Commercial growth need not advance workers
st.an: The source presents LPO growth as accompanied by an attractive professional path, regular corporate-client interaction and prominent legal work. It therefore pushes against the cluster’s worker-focused distinction between commercial expansion and substantive professional advancement, although it offers promotional company-level claims rather than evidence about transferable capital or industry-wide outcomes.
qs: It continues to be a wonderful alternative career path for Indian attorneys.
It allows them to interact with the legal departments of large companies day in and out.

st.t: Legal outsourcing: Acquisition joined content with delivery
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s proposition that Pangea3 combined legal-service delivery with Thomson Reuters’ content and software strategy. It provides a concrete US–India delivery example while explicitly presenting integration benefits as prospective rather than demonstrated; its broader value-creation claim remains anecdotal rather than market-wide evidence.
qs: But it is the promise of how we as a service company can combine with their content and software to create robust solutions for the industry (Thomson Reuters owns Westlaw, a legal database).
We have two employees who are with them on the ground in New York and 30 people in Mumbai are a support team.

kp.k: LPO growth expands alternative legal-service delivery
kp.d: In this 2014 interview, Pangea3's managing director estimates the legal process outsourcing industry at $500 million to $1 billion with double digit CAGR. The speaker reports Pangea3's employee count rising from 540 at Thomson Reuters' November 2010 acquisition to 1,000, and law-firm business growing about 100 percent year over year. These are interviewee-reported market and company figures, not findings about AI.
qs: The legal process outsourcing industry (LPO) is estimated between $500 million and $1 billion today, with double digit CAGR.
When Thomson Reuters acquired Pangea3 in November 2010, we had 540 employees and today we have 1,000.
We are the fastest growing business within Thomson Reuters Legal and our business with law firms year over year is up about 100 percent.

kp.k: Outsourcing offers Indian attorneys an alternative career path
kp.d: The managing director presents LPO employment as an alternative career path for Indian attorneys, involving daily interaction with large companies' legal departments and work on prominent matters. This is the speaker's characterization of career opportunities, rather than evidence about training outcomes or professional progression.
qs: It continues to be a wonderful alternative career path for Indian attorneys.
It allows them to interact with the legal departments of large companies day in and out.
They work on matters that the The Wall Street Journal reports on its front page.

kp.k: India's lawyer supply underpins its claimed outsourcing advantage
kp.d: Asked about competition from other countries, the managing director argues that India's intellectual capacity and volume of lawyers sustain its advantage. The speaker describes healthy growth among top-tier providers and continued start-up formation despite an earlier expectation that start-ups would die down; no comparative market data are supplied.
qs: There is a top tier of companies that are growing and healthy.
There are also a lot of start-up LPOs that we thought would die down, but they are still being set up.
There has been noise from the Philippines, eastern Europe, South Africa and Israel, but there is no answer to the depth of intellectual capacity and numbers of lawyers India is putting out.

kp.k: Growth combines broader services with changing buyer acceptance
kp.d: The managing director expects growth both from reaching law firms and corporate legal departments and from broadening services. The speaker describes previously unreceptive law firms becoming interested and general counsel pushing their firms to use outsourcing, characterizing the market's direction as a shift from cost reduction to value creation. These are qualitative observations and expectations rather than quantified adoption findings.
qs: Both. Every LPO in India has called the top corporate legal departments and law firms in Europe and the US, but the market continues to change.
The law firm that hung up on one of our sales people six months ago is now calling us.
The general counsel who was not comfortable with us doing electronic discovery [electronic exchange of litigation date] is now pushing his law firm to use us for every electronic delivery.
The market is shifting from cost reduction to value creation.

kp.k: Distributed teams perform document review and complex fact-finding
kp.d: As a concrete engagement example, the managing director describes supporting a large law firm on a criminal matter in a US federal court. Pangea3 had performed document review for the preceding year-and-a-half, with two employees on the ground in New York and 30 supporting them in Mumbai, where complex fact-finding tasks were performed daily. The example documents geographic distribution of legal work, without attributing it to AI or reporting measured cost or quality outcomes.
qs: One of the most exciting engagements we are working on is for a large law firm working on a criminal matter in a US federal court.
We have been doing document review on this matter for the last year-and-a-half.
We have two employees who are with them on the ground in New York and 30 people in Mumbai are a support team.
At the end of every day, there are complex fact-finding tasks that are being done out of Mumbai.

kp.k: Services, content and software integration promises future solutions
kp.d: The managing director frames Thomson Reuters' acquisition as an opportunity to combine Pangea3's service delivery with the parent's content and software; the document identifies Westlaw as a Thomson Reuters legal database. This is a prospective strategic claim about integrated legal solutions, not a demonstrated outcome or an explicit AI strategy.
qs: In 2010, when Thomson Reuters wanted a presence in this business, they scoured the industry and found us as one of the fastest growing companies.
But it is the promise of how we as a service company can combine with their content and software to create robust solutions for the industry (Thomson Reuters owns Westlaw, a legal database).
So the best is yet to come.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The source makes no explicit claims about AI. Its claims concern legal process outsourcing (LPO), which the interviewed Pangea3 managing director portrays as growing, increasingly value-oriented, and likely to benefit from combining services with content and software.
pts.d: In Samar Srivastava's interview, the Pangea3 managing director claims that India retains an advantage over competing outsourcing locations because of its intellectual capacity and supply of lawyers. The speaker expects further growth from both expanding relationships with law firms and corporate legal departments and broadening services. The speaker also anticipates more robust solutions from combining Pangea3's services with Thomson Reuters' content and software. These are outsourcing and service-integration claims, not claims about AI automation or lawyer replacement.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The speaker supports the outsourcing-growth claims with market estimates, reported company growth, buyer anecdotes, and an ongoing litigation-support engagement.
pts.d: The managing director estimates the LPO market at $500 million–$1 billion with double-digit compound annual growth, reports headcount rising from 540 at acquisition to 1,000, and reports approximately 100 percent year-over-year growth in business with law firms. No underlying datasets or calculation methods are supplied. Changing buyer attitudes are illustrated through anecdotes about law firms and general counsel. A US federal criminal matter illustrates delivery beyond basic document review: two employees work in New York with a 30-person Mumbai support team undertaking complex fact-finding. India's comparative advantage and the future benefits of service/content/software integration are asserted without a comparative study or measured outcomes.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Present-tense claims refer to the January 2014 publication context; future growth and integration benefits have no specified deadline.
pts.d: Headcount growth is measured from the November 2010 acquisition to the interview's present. Law-firm business growth is described as year over year without a precise reporting period. The buyer-conversion anecdote spans six months, and the litigation document-review engagement had lasted a year and a half. Continued growth is linked to both client expansion and broader services; anticipated integration benefits depend on combining Pangea3's service capabilities with Thomson Reuters' content and software. The speaker distinguishes a growing, healthy top tier from continuing startup entry rather than supplying evidence that all LPO providers are equally successful.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The identified beneficiaries and market participants are Indian attorneys, LPO providers, law firms, corporate legal departments, and Thomson Reuters.
pts.d: The managing director presents LPO as an alternative career path for Indian attorneys, offering direct interaction with major corporate legal departments and participation in prominent matters. European and US law firms and corporate legal departments are described as increasingly receptive buyers, with general counsel encouraging outside firms to use outsourced services. Pangea3's distributed litigation team illustrates how law firms receive offshore document-review and fact-finding support. Competing outsourcing locations are portrayed as lacking India's depth of legal talent. The source does not claim AI-driven employment displacement or access-to-justice effects.
